claim: Elevated glucose increases vascular reactivity by promoting L-type CaV1.2 channel (LTCC) activity by protein kinase A (PKA).
source: Elevated glucose increases vascular reactivity by promoting L-type CaV1.2 channel (LTCC) activity by protein kinase A (PKA).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that sets up the research question.

claim: P2Y11 is the only Gs-coupled P2Y receptor.
source: Using human tissue, expression for P2Y11, the only Gs-coupled P2Y receptor, was detected in nanometer proximity to CaV1.2 and PKA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The selective P2Y11 agonist NF546 stimulates cAMP production in human arterial myocytes.
source: FRET-based experiments revealed that the selective P2Y11 agonist NF546 and elevated glucose stimulate cAMP production resulting in enhanced PKA-dependent LTCC activity.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elevated glucose stimulates cAMP production in human arterial myocytes.
source: FRET-based experiments revealed that the selective P2Y11 agonist NF546 and elevated glucose stimulate cAMP production resulting in enhanced PKA-dependent LTCC activity.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NF546 and elevated glucose-induced cAMP production results in enhanced PKA-dependent LTCC activity.
source: FRET-based experiments revealed that the selective P2Y11 agonist NF546 and elevated glucose stimulate cAMP production resulting in enhanced PKA-dependent LTCC activity.
evidence: This is supported by FRET and electrophysiology data in the manuscript.

claim: The selective P2Y11 inhibitor NF340 blocks the effects of NF546 and elevated glucose on cAMP production and LTCC activity.
source: These changes were blocked by the selective P2Y11 inhibitor NF340.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NF340 prevents glucose and NF546 effects.

claim: P2Y11 is expressed in nanometer proximity to CaV1.2 in human arterial myocytes.
source: Using human tissue, expression for P2Y11, the only Gs-coupled P2Y receptor, was detected in nanometer proximity to CaV1.2 and PKA.
evidence: This is supported by GSD super-resolution microscopy and PLA data.

claim: P2Y11 is expressed in nanometer proximity to PKA in human arterial myocytes.
source: Using human tissue, expression for P2Y11, the only Gs-coupled P2Y receptor, was detected in nanometer proximity to CaV1.2 and PKA.
evidence: This is supported by GSD super-resolution microscopy and PLA data.

claim: A P2Y11-like receptor mediates the glucose response in mouse arterial myocytes.
source: Comparable results were observed in mouse tissue, suggesting that a P2Y11-like receptor is mediating the glucose response in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by comparable functional data in mouse tissue using pharmacological tools.

claim: P2Y11 plays a key role in regulating PKA-dependent LTCC function and vascular reactivity during diabetic hyperglycemia.
source: These findings established a key role for P2Y11 in regulating PKA-dependent LTCC function and vascular reactivity during diabetic hyperglycemia.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data.

claim: Diabetes is a major risk factor contributing to cardiovascular complications, including hypertension, increased risk of stroke, coronary disease, and organ failure.
source: Diabetes is a major risk factor contributing to cardiovascular complications, including hypertension, increased risk of stroke, coronary disease, and organ failure (Whelton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Cardiovascular complications in diabetes are often linked to the effects of elevated extracellular glucose on vascular function.
source: These complications are often linked to the effects of elevated extracellular glucose (e.g. hyperglycemia - the hallmark metabolic abnormality in diabetes) on vascular function (Brown et al., 2010; Cooper et al., 2001; Tousoulis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Enhanced contractility of arterial myocytes is a critical contributing factor to diabetic vascular complications.
source: In addition to endothelium-dependent alterations (Lagaud et al., 2001; Sena et al., 2013), endothelium-independent modifications, including enhanced contractility of arterial myocytes, are emerging as critical contributing factors to these complications (Aronson, 2008; DeFronzo et al., 2013; Fleischhacker et al., 1999; Montero et al., 2013; Nieves-Cintrón et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Augmented vasoconstriction in response to acute and chronic elevations in extracellular glucose is independent of endothelial function.
source: Consistent with this notion, we and others recently demonstrated augmented vasoconstriction in response to acute and chronic elevations in extracellular glucose that were independent of endothelial function (Fleischhacker et al., 1999; Jackson et al., 2016; Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research including the authors' own work.

claim: Glucose-mediated effects on vascular reactivity are linked to an increase in L-type CaV1.2 channel (LTCC) activity in human and murine arterial myocytes.
source: We linked these glucose-mediated effects on vascular reactivity to an increase in L-type CaV1.2 channel (LTCC) activity in human and murine arterial myocytes (Navedo et al., 2010b; Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' prior research.

claim: Ca2+ influx via LTCCs is the main Ca2+ entry pathway in arterial myocytes and determines muscle contractility and arterial diameter.
source: This is critical, as Ca2+ influx via LTCCs is the main Ca2+ entry pathway in these cells and determines muscle contractility and arterial diameter (Knot and Nelson, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Glucose-mediated potentiation of LTCCs involves phosphorylation of CaV1.2 at serine 1928 (Ser1928) by protein kinase A (PKA).
source: Unexpectedly, we found that glucose-mediated potentiation of LTCCs involves phosphorylation of CaV1.2 at serine 1928 (Ser1928) by protein kinase A (PKA) (Morotti et al., 2017; Navedo et al., 2010b; Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' prior research.

claim: Elevations in cellular glucose trigger autocrine release of nucleotides (e.g. ATP, UTP) into the extracellular space of many cells, including arterial myocytes.
source: Elevations in cellular glucose have been shown to trigger autocrine release of nucleotides (e.g. ATP, UTP) into the extracellular space of many cells, including arterial myocytes (Costa et al., 2009; Hazama et al., 1998; Nilsson et al., 2006; Parodi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Extracellular nucleotides can act on G protein-coupled P2Y receptors to induce a plethora of cellular responses.
source: These extracellular nucleotides can then act on G protein-coupled P2Y receptors to induce a plethora of cellular responses (von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Elevations in extracellular glucose led to increases in intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) in isolated arterial myocytes.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that elevations in extracellular glucose led to increases in intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) in isolated arterial myocytes (Nilsson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The glucose-mediated increase in intracellular Ca2+ was associated with enhanced autocrine release of nucleotides engaging P2Y receptors.
source: Indeed, this glucose-mediated response was associated with enhanced autocrine release of nucleotides engaging P2Y receptors, but the contributing mechanisms as well as the identity of the P2Y receptor involved are unclear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research, though the mechanisms remain unclear.

claim: Eight functionally diverse G protein-coupled P2Y receptors have been identified.
source: Eight functionally diverse G protein-coupled P2Y receptors have been identified (von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Most P2Y receptors are coupled to Gq/i proteins.
source: Most of these P2Y receptors are coupled to Gq/i proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P2Y receptor signaling.

claim: P2Y11 is the only P2Y receptor that is coupled to Gs.
source: Conversely, P2Y11 is the only P2Y receptor that is coupled to Gs (Communi et al., 1997; Kennedy, 2017; Schuchardt et al., 2012; von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Activation of P2Y11 could activate adenylyl cyclase (AC) and PKA.
source: Activation of this receptor could then activate adenylyl cyclase (AC) and PKA to underlie the glucose-induced effects on LTCC activity, but its role in arterial myocytes is unclear.
evidence: This is inferred from the known signaling pathway of Gs-coupled receptors.

claim: P2Y11 receptors were first cloned from human tissue and subsequently identified in other species.
source: P2Y11 receptors were first cloned from human tissue and subsequently identified in other species (Kennedy, 2017; von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The P2Y11 gene has not been found at the expected position in the mouse genome.
source: Although the P2Y11 gene has not been found at the expected position in the mouse genome, recent rodent annotations related to this gene (e.g. XM_008766009.2 and XM_0130655917.2), as well as studies defining a functional role based on pharmacological data obtained from rat and mouse tissue hinted at the presence of at least a P2Y11-like receptor in mice (Kennedy, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and genomic database information.

claim: Recent rodent annotations and pharmacological studies hint at the presence of at least a P2Y11-like receptor in mice.
source: Although the P2Y11 gene has not been found at the expected position in the mouse genome, recent rodent annotations related to this gene (e.g. XM_008766009.2 and XM_0130655917.2), as well as studies defining a functional role based on pharmacological data obtained from rat and mouse tissue hinted at the presence of at least a P2Y11-like receptor in mice (Kennedy, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature and genomic annotations.

claim: Increasing extracellular glucose from 10 mM to 20 mM D-glucose caused significant constriction in pressurized mouse cerebral arteries.
source: When increasing extracellular glucose from 10 mM to 20 mM D-glucose, there was a significant constriction (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1 and 2), which is consistent with previous reports by our group and others (Jackson et al., 2016; Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and cited prior research.

claim: Apyrase-treated arteries failed to constrict to 20 mM D-glucose.
source: Apyrase-treated arteries failed to constrict to 20 mM D-glucose (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Vasoconstriction in response to 60 mM potassium (K+) was similar in control and apyrase-treated arteries.
source: Vasoconstriction in response to 60 mM potassium (K+) in which the membrane potential closely follows the equilibrium potential for K+ (~−20 mV) (Knot and Nelson, 1998), was similar in control and apyrase-treated arteries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and a citation.

claim: The glucose-induced constriction was not attributed to changes in osmolarity.
source: Furthermore, the glucose-induced constriction was not attributed to changes in osmolarity as treatment with equimolar concentrations of the nonpermeable mannitol (20 mM = 10 mM D-glucose +10 mM mannitol) had no effect on vascular reactivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B using mannitol as an osmotic control.

claim: 20 mM D-glucose significantly enhanced IBa in wild type control arterial myocytes.
source: We found that 20 mM D-glucose significantly enhanced IBa in wild type (wt) control arterial myocytes, but not in apyrase-treated cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 20 mM D-glucose did not enhance IBa in apyrase-treated arterial myocytes.
source: We found that 20 mM D-glucose significantly enhanced IBa in wild type (wt) control arterial myocytes, but not in apyrase-treated cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The glucose effect on LTCC activity was not due to changes in osmolarity.
source: The glucose effect on LTCC activity was not due to changes in osmolarity as 20 mM mannitol had no impact on IBa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C using mannitol as an osmotic control.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser1928 at CaV1.2 increased in response to 20 mM D-glucose in control arterial lysates.
source: Data revealed increased phosphorylation of this residue in response to 20 mM D-glucose in control arterial lysates (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Glucose-induced Ser1928 phosphorylation was hindered in lysates from apyrase-treated arteries.
source: Moreover, glucose-induced Ser1928 phosphorylation was hindered in lysates from apyrase-treated arteries (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Glucose-induced Ser1928 phosphorylation was absent in arterial lysates exposed to 20 mM mannitol.
source: However, this response was completely absent in arterial lysates exposed to 20 mM mannitol, thus ruling out any osmolarity effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: IBa was significantly elevated in arterial myocytes exposed to 20 mM D-glucose under static bath conditions.
source: Conversely, IBa was significantly elevated in arterial myocytes exposed to 20 mM D-glucose when the bath perfusion was stopped (e.g. static bath conditions).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: IBa was statistically similar in cells exposed to 10 mM and 20 mM D-glucose under continuous bath perfusion.
source: We found statistically similar IBa in cells exposed to 10 mM and 20 mM D-glucose under continuous bath perfusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: An immunoreactive band of the expected molecular weight for P2Y11 (~40 kDa) was detected in lysates from freshly dissected human adipose arteries.
source: We subsequently detected an immunoreactive band of the expected molecular weight for P2Y11 (~40 kDa) in lysates from freshly dissected human adipose arteries (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of human arteries with specific human P2Y11 antisense ODNs knocked down ~50% of the basal P2Y11 protein abundance.
source: This band seems specific for P2Y11 since treatment of human arteries with specific human P2Y11 antisense ODNs knocked down ~50% of the basal P2Y11 protein abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B using antisense ODN knockdown.

claim: P2Y11 has a prominent distribution on the surface membrane of freshly dissociated human arterial myocytes.
source: Confocal imaging and line profile analysis of P2Y11-associated fluorescence and the plasma membrane marker wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) suggest a prominent distribution of the receptor on the surface membrane of freshly dissociated human arterial myocytes (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: An immunoreactive band of the expected molecular weight for P2Y11 was detected in mouse arterial lysates.
source: We observed comparable results in mouse arterial lysates and arterial myocytes, including detection and knock down with P2Y11 ODNs of an immunoreactive band of the expected molecular weight for P2Y11 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B and D.

claim: A band of ~110–120 kDa was observed in mouse arterial lysates, perhaps reflecting the formation of heterodimers between the P2Y11 receptor itself or other purinergic/G protein-coupled receptors.
source: A band of ~110–120 kDa was observed in mouse arterial lysates, perhaps reflecting the formation of heterodimers between the P2Y11 receptor itself or other purinergic/G protein-coupled receptors, as previously reported (Barragán-Iglesias et al., 2015; Barragán-Iglesias et al., 2014; Ecke et al., 2008; Nishimura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot observation and citations to literature on receptor dimerization.

claim: P2Y11-like-associated fluorescence is distributed at the surface membrane of mouse arterial myocytes.
source: We also found expected distribution of P2Y11-like-associated fluorescence at the surface membrane of mouse arterial myocytes (Figure 2D and E), which was not observed when the primary antibody was omitted or boiled (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2D and E, with negative controls in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E.

claim: P2Y11, CaV1.2, and PKAcat form clusters of various sizes at the sarcolemma of human arterial myocytes.
source: The GSD super-resolution localization maps (Figure 3A and B, bottom panels) for P2Y11, CaV1.2, and PKAcat obtained from conventional TIRF images (Figure 3A and B, top panels) showed that these proteins form clusters of various sizes (Figure 3C) and density (Figure 3D) at the sarcolemma of human arterial myocytes.
evidence: This is supported by GSD super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Merged spatial maps of P2Y11 with CaV1.2 or PKAcat suggested a close association between a subset of these proteins.
source: Whereas clusters were broadly expressed throughout the sarcolemma, merged spatial maps of P2Y11 with CaV1.2 or PKAcat suggested a close association between a subset of these proteins (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by GSD super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The closest centroids for P2Y11-CaV1.2 were at 59 nm.
source: Indeed, histograms of the P2Y11-to-nearest CaV1.2 or PKAcat distances revealed that the closest centroids for P2Y11-CaV1.2 and P2Y11- PKAcat were at 59 nm and 58 nm, respectively (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis from GSD super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The closest centroids for P2Y11-PKAcat were at 58 nm.
source: Indeed, histograms of the P2Y11-to-nearest CaV1.2 or PKAcat distances revealed that the closest centroids for P2Y11-CaV1.2 and P2Y11- PKAcat were at 59 nm and 58 nm, respectively (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by distance analysis from GSD super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Similar results for P2Y11, CaV1.2, and PKAcat clustering and proximity were observed using freshly dissociated mouse cerebral arterial myocytes.
source: Similar results were observed using freshly dissociated mouse cerebral arterial myocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by GSD super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The percentage of overlap between P2Y11-CaV1.2 and P2Y11-PKAcat obtained from the experimental localization maps was significantly higher than that observed for a simulated random distribution.
source: Our analysis found that the percentage of overlap between P2Y11-CaV1.2 and P2Y11-PKAcat obtained from the experimental localization maps was significantly higher than that observed for a simulated random distribution between P2Y11-CaV1.2 and P2Y11-PKAcat (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of GSD super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Robust fluorescent puncta were detected in human arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and CaV1.2 using proximity ligation assay (PLA).
source: Whereas PLA signals were absent when at least one primary antibody was omitted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), robust fluorescent puncta were detected in human (Figure 4A and B) and mouse (Figure 4C and D) arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and CaV1.2 or P2Y11 and PKAcat.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Robust fluorescent puncta were detected in human arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and PKAcat using proximity ligation assay (PLA).
source: Whereas PLA signals were absent when at least one primary antibody was omitted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), robust fluorescent puncta were detected in human (Figure 4A and B) and mouse (Figure 4C and D) arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and CaV1.2 or P2Y11 and PKAcat.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Robust fluorescent puncta were detected in mouse arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and CaV1.2 using proximity ligation assay (PLA).
source: Whereas PLA signals were absent when at least one primary antibody was omitted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), robust fluorescent puncta were detected in human (Figure 4A and B) and mouse (Figure 4C and D) arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and CaV1.2 or P2Y11 and PKAcat.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Robust fluorescent puncta were detected in mouse arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and PKAcat using proximity ligation assay (PLA).
source: Whereas PLA signals were absent when at least one primary antibody was omitted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), robust fluorescent puncta were detected in human (Figure 4A and B) and mouse (Figure 4C and D) arterial myocytes co-labeled for P2Y11 and CaV1.2 or P2Y11 and PKAcat.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Human P2Y11 or mouse P2Y11-like receptors are located on the surface membrane of arterial myocytes within nanometer proximity (~≤40 nm) of a subpopulation of CaV1.2 and PKAcat.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that human P2Y11 or mouse P2Y11-like receptors are located on the surface membrane of arterial myocytes within nanometer proximity (~≤40 nm) of a subpopulation of CaV1.2 and PKAcat.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GSD super-resolution microscopy and PLA data.

claim: The highly selective P2Y11 agonist NF546 (500 nM) increased cAMP synthesis in tsA-201 cells.
source: As expected, the highly selective P2Y11 agonist NF546 (500 nM) (Meis et al., 2010) increased cAMP synthesis in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data in tsA-201 cells described in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The NF546-induced cAMP response remained intact in tsA-201 cells pretreated with selective P2Y1 (10 µM MRS2179) or P2Y6 (100 nM MRS2578) inhibitors.
source: This NF546-induced cAMP response remained intact in cells pretreated with either selective P2Y1 (10 µM MRS2179) or P2Y6 (100 nM MRS2578) inhibitors but was prevented in cells exposed to the selective P2Y11 inhibitor NF340 (10 µM; 500-fold more selective for P2Y11 than other P2Y receptors) (Meis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data in tsA-201 cells described in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The NF546-induced cAMP response was prevented in tsA-201 cells exposed to the selective P2Y11 inhibitor NF340 (10 µM).
source: This NF546-induced cAMP response remained intact in cells pretreated with either selective P2Y1 (10 µM MRS2179) or P2Y6 (100 nM MRS2578) inhibitors but was prevented in cells exposed to the selective P2Y11 inhibitor NF340 (10 µM; 500-fold more selective for P2Y11 than other P2Y receptors) (Meis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data in tsA-201 cells described in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NF546 increased cAMP synthesis in primary, unpassaged human arterial myocytes expressing the ICUE3-PM sensor.
source: We recapitulated the NF546-induced cAMP response and its ablation by pretreatment with NF340 in primary, unpassaged human arterial myocytes expressing the ICUE3-PM sensor (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Pretreatment with NF340 ablated the NF546-induced cAMP response in primary, unpassaged human arterial myocytes.
source: We recapitulated the NF546-induced cAMP response and its ablation by pretreatment with NF340 in primary, unpassaged human arterial myocytes expressing the ICUE3-PM sensor (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Increasing D-glucose concentration from 5 mM to 15 mM induced a small yet significant increase in cAMP synthesis in human arterial myocytes.
source: Increasing D-glucose concentration from 5 mM to 15 mM, which are glucose concentrations comparable to those observed in nondiabetic and diabetic patients respectively, induced a small yet significant increase in cAMP synthesis in human cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The glucose effects on cAMP synthesis are not due to osmotic changes.
source: The glucose effects are not due to osmotic changes as equimolar concentrations of the non-permeable mannitol did not induce any cAMP synthesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B using mannitol as an osmotic control.

claim: Simultaneous application of 15 mM D-glucose +NF546 resulted in cAMP synthesis of a similar magnitude to that induced by independent treatments.
source: Simultaneous application of 15 mM D-glucose +NF546 resulted in cAMP synthesis of a similar magnitude to that induced by independent treatments (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Application of NF546 by itself or 15 mM D-glucose +NF546 failed to induce cAMP synthesis in human arterial myocytes pretreated with NF340.
source: Consistent with this notion, application of NF546 by itself or 15 mM D-glucose +NF546 failed to induce cAMP synthesis in cells pretreated with NF340 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Forskolin was able to stimulate global cAMP production in human arterial myocytes even after NF340 pretreatment.
source: Yet forskolin, which bypasses P2Y11, was still able to stimulate global cAMP production.
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data described in the text and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Similar cAMP synthesis results were observed in murine arterial myocytes expressing the ICUE3-PM sensor.
source: Similar results were observed in murine arterial myocytes expressing the ICUE3-PM sensor (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by FRET-based cAMP imaging data shown in Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: cAMP synthesis in response to elevated glucose and the P2Y11 agonist NF546 was significantly larger in human myocytes compared to mouse cells.
source: Intriguingly, cAMP synthesis in response to elevated glucose and the P2Y11 agonist NF546 was significantly larger in human myocytes compared to mouse cells (glucose: 0.077 ± 0.003 in human vs 0.045 ± 0.002 in mouse; NF546: 0.083 ± 0.005 in human vs 0.045 ± 0.004 in mouse; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison of FRET-based cAMP imaging data between human and mouse cells.

claim: Elevating extracellular glucose from 5 mM to 15 mM stimulates LTCC activity in human arterial myocytes.
source: In our next series of experiments, we confirmed the glucose-induced increase in IBa detected in mouse arterial myocytes (Figure 1B) using freshly dissociated human arterial myocytes in which external glucose was elevated from 5 mM to 15 mM (Figure 6A and B). These results indicate that elevations in extracellular glucose also stimulate LTCC activity in human arterial myocytes (Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A and B and a citation to prior work.

claim: The increase in IBa evoked by 15 mM D-glucose was prevented in human arterial myocytes pretreated with NF340.
source: The increase in IBa evoked by 15 mM D-glucose was prevented in human cells pretreated with NF340 (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Glucose-induced potentiation of IBa was prevented in mouse arterial myocytes pretreated with NF340.
source: Glucose-induced potentiation of IBa was also prevented in mouse arterial myocytes pretreated with NF340 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Inhibition of P2Y6 receptors with MRS2578 failed to stop the increase in IBa in response to 20 mM D-glucose in mouse arterial myocytes.
source: However, inhibition of P2Y6 receptors with MRS2578, which has been implicated in myogenic tone regulation and glucose-induced NFAT activation in arterial myocytes (Brayden et al., 2013; Nilsson et al., 2006), failed to stop the increase in IBa in response to 20 mM D-glucose (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C and D and citations to prior work.

claim: Basal IBa were similar in mouse arterial myocytes exposed to 10 mM D-glucose and 10 mM D-glucose +MRS2578.
source: Note that basal IBa were similar in cells exposed to 10 mM D-glucose and 10 mM D-glucose +MRS2578, suggesting that inhibition of P2Y6 did not alter basal LTCC activity (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Elevating extracellular glucose from 5 mM to 15 mM significantly increased Ser1928 phosphorylation in human arterial lysates.
source: As observed in mouse arteries (Figure 1C), we found that elevating extracellular glucose significantly increased Ser1928 phosphorylation in human arterial lysates (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Glucose-mediated increase in Ser1928 phosphorylation was prevented if human arterial lysates were pretreated with NF340.
source: Yet, this glucose-mediated increase in Ser1928 phosphorylation was prevented if arterial lysates were pretreated with NF340, whereas phosphorylation still occurred if arterial lysates were pretreated with the P2Y6 inhibitor MRS2578 (Figure 6E and F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E and F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Glucose-mediated increase in Ser1928 phosphorylation still occurred if mouse arterial lysates were pretreated with the P2Y6 inhibitor MRS2578.
source: Yet, this glucose-mediated increase in Ser1928 phosphorylation was prevented if arterial lysates were pretreated with NF340, whereas phosphorylation still occurred if arterial lysates were pretreated with the P2Y6 inhibitor MRS2578 (Figure 6E and F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E and F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Vasoconstriction in response to elevated glucose was blocked in pressurized mouse cerebral arteries exposed to NF340.
source: Furthermore, vasoconstriction in response to elevated glucose was blocked in pressurized (60 mmHg) mouse cerebral arteries exposed to NF340 (Figure 6G and H and Supplementary file 2) but not to MRS2578 (Figure 6I and J and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Vasoconstriction in response to elevated glucose was not blocked in pressurized mouse cerebral arteries exposed to MRS2578.
source: Furthermore, vasoconstriction in response to elevated glucose was blocked in pressurized (60 mmHg) mouse cerebral arteries exposed to NF340 (Figure 6G and H and Supplementary file 2) but not to MRS2578 (Figure 6I and J and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Arterial tone was reduced in arteries exposed to MRS2578.
source: Note that while arterial tone was similar in control and NF340-treated arteries, it was reduced in arteries exposed to MRS2578 (Figure 6I and J), which is in line with recent data showing that P2Y6 is a sensor of pressure-induced constriction (Brayden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 6I and J and a citation to prior work.

claim: Vasoconstriction in response to 60 mM K+ was similar in control and NF340 as well as MRS2578-treated arteries.
source: Vasoconstriction in response to 60 mM K+ was similar in control and NF340 as well as MRS2578-treated arteries (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The glucose-induced vasoconstriction was not altered by adding the selective P2Y1 inhibitor MRS2179 (10 μM) either before or after 20 mM D-glucose stimulation.
source: Data revealed that the glucose-induced vasoconstriction was not altered by adding the selective P2Y1 inhibitor MRS2179 (10 μM) either before or after 20 mM D-glucose stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E and Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: IBa was significantly increased by application of NF546 in freshly dissociated human arterial myocytes.
source: Using freshly dissociated human arterial myocytes, we found that IBa was significantly increased by application of NF546 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: NF546 increased IBa at multiple membrane potentials in mouse arterial myocytes with no change in the current-voltage (I-V) relationship.
source: This P2Y11 agonist also increased IBa at multiple membrane potentials in mouse arterial myocytes with no change in the current-voltage (I-V) relationship (Vmax = 14.9 ± 2.0 mV for 10 mM D-glucose and Vmax = 10.9 ± 1.1 mV for NF546; p=0.1085, extra sum-of-squares F test) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The NF546-mediated increase in IBa was similar in magnitude to that induced by elevated glucose.
source: The NF546-mediated increase in IBa was similar in magnitude to that induced by elevated glucose (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Similar IBa potentiation was observed after application of the non-hydrolyzed ATP analog and potent P2Y11 agonist ATPγS (1 μM).
source: Similar IBa potentiation was also observed after application of the non-hydrolyzed ATP analog and potent P2Y11 agonist ATPγS (1 μM; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) (von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and a citation.

claim: NF546 elevated Ser1928 phosphorylation in freshly dissected human and mouse arterial lysates.
source: We further correlated the potentiation in IBa by NF546 to an elevation of Ser1928 phosphorylation in freshly dissected human and mouse arterial lysates (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NF546 failed to upregulate IBa in arterial myocytes incubated with the PKA inhibitors PKI (100 nM) or rpcAMP (10 μM).
source: Consistent with a key role for PKA, NF546 failed to upregulate IBa in arterial myocytes incubated with the PKA inhibitors PKI (100 nM) or rpcAMP (10 μM) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pressurized arteries showed significant constriction upon NF546 application.
source: Accordingly, pressurized (60 mmHg) arteries that developed stable arterial tone and responded to 60 mM K+ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1 and 2) showed significant constriction upon NF546 application (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: NF546 did not induce further constriction in wt arteries previously exposed to 20 mM D-glucose.
source: Interestingly, NF546 did not induce further constriction in wt arteries previously exposed to 20 mM D-glucose (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Arterial tone was similar in arteries treated with 20 mM D-glucose or 20 mM D-glucose +NF546.
source: Indeed, arterial tone was similar in arteries treated with 20 mM D-glucose or 20 mM D-glucose +NF546 (Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data described in the text and Supplementary files.

claim: Arteries from a S1928A knockin mouse failed to constrict to NF546.
source: Confirming a critical role for Ser1928, arteries from a S1928A knockin mouse in which phosphorylation of this CaV1.2 amino acid is prevented (Lemke et al., 2008; Nystoriak et al., 2017; Qian et al., 2017), failed to constrict to NF546 (Figure 7F and Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 7F and citations to prior work.

claim: Response of S1928A arteries to 60 mM K+ was similar to those observed for wt arteries.
source: Response of S1928A arteries to 60 mM K+ was similar to those observed for wt arteries (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by arterial diameter measurement data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Wt cells isolated from the 20 mM D-glucose treated group had significantly enhanced LTCC open probability (nPo) compared to those in the 10 mM D-glucose group.
source: We found that wt cells isolated from the 20 mM D-glucose but not the 20 mM mannitol treated group had significantly enhanced LTCC open probability (nPo) compared to those in the 10 mM D-glucose group (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Wt cells isolated from the 20 mM mannitol treated group did not have significantly enhanced LTCC open probability (nPo) compared to those in the 10 mM D-glucose group.
source: We found that wt cells isolated from the 20 mM D-glucose but not the 20 mM mannitol treated group had significantly enhanced LTCC open probability (nPo) compared to those in the 10 mM D-glucose group (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The increase in LTCC activity during diabetic hyperglycemia was prevented in arterial myocytes from arteries treated in the presence of the P2Y11 inhibitor NF340.
source: This increase in LTCC activity during diabetic hyperglycemia, however, was prevented in arterial myocytes from arteries treated in the presence of the P2Y11 inhibitor NF340.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel electrophysiology data described in the text and shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Ser1928 phosphorylation was significantly elevated in arteries chronically exposed to 20 mM D-glucose.
source: Ser1928 phosphorylation was significantly elevated in arteries chronically exposed to 20 mM D-glucose, but this effect was completely abolished in the presence of NF340 (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The glucose-induced elevation of Ser1928 phosphorylation was completely abolished in the presence of NF340.
source: Ser1928 phosphorylation was significantly elevated in arteries chronically exposed to 20 mM D-glucose, but this effect was completely abolished in the presence of NF340 (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LTCC nPo was similar in arterial myocytes from S1928A arteries incubated for 48 hr in 10 mM or 20 mM D-glucose.
source: Consistent with a key role for Ser1928 phosphorylation in potentiation of LTCC activity in response to chronic elevations in glucose, LTCC nPo was similar in arterial myocytes from S1928A arteries incubated for 48 hr in 10 mM or 20 mM D-glucose (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PKA activity has been traditionally associated with vasodilation due, in part, to increased K+ channel activity.
source: Our findings indicating that elevated extracellular glucose triggers PKA-dependent potentiation of LTCC activity to induce vasoconstriction were unexpected, as PKA activity has been traditionally associated with vasodilation due, in part, to increased K+ channel activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Glucose could influence LTCCs via a cAMP/PKA signaling pathway that is distinct from that governing K+ channels as occurs upon β adrenergic stimulation.
source: A reasonable prediction was that glucose could influence LTCCs via a cAMP/PKA signaling pathway that is distinct from that governing K+ channels as occurs upon β adrenergic stimulation (Moore et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge and a citation.

claim: Optimal ion channel regulation by effector proteins is constrained by their nanometer distance between each other.
source: Indeed, Tajada et al recently showed that optimal ion channel regulation by effector proteins is constrained by their nanometer distance between each other (Tajada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A subpopulation of CaV1.2 (~10% of CaV1.2 clusters) is in nanometer proximity to pools of PKA.
source: In support of this possibility, our recent work revealed nanometer proximity of a subpopulation of CaV1.2 (~10% of CaV1.2 clusters) to pools of PKA (Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior research.

claim: P2Y11 may be in close proximity to a specific AC isoform in arterial myocytes.
source: Moreover, given the cAMP biosensor data demonstrating that both glucose and the P2Y11 agonist NF546 induce localized subsarcolemmal cAMP synthesis (Figure 5), it is also likely that P2Y11 may be in close proximity to a specific AC isoform in arterial myocytes - the identity of which remains to be established.
evidence: This is inferred from the cAMP biosensor data and the known signaling pathway.

claim: A distinctive nanomolecular domain likely contains P2Y11, AC, PKA and CaV1.2 in arterial myocytes.
source: Nevertheless, this implicates the formation of a distinctive nanomolecular domain likely containing P2Y11, AC, PKA and CaV1.2 in arterial myocytes (Figure 8D), although its confirmation is beyond the scope of this study.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data on protein proximity and signaling.

claim: This nanodomain may ensure the necessary signaling compartmentalization required for PKA-mediated effects on LTCC activity and vascular reactivity in response to elevated glucose.
source: This nanodomain may ensure the necessary signaling compartmentalization required for PKA-mediated effects on LTCC activity and vascular reactivity in response to elevated glucose.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and known principles of signaling compartmentalization.

claim: The spatial organization of the P2Y11/AC/PKA/CaV1.2 nanodomain could be facilitated by scaffold proteins, such as A kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs).
source: The spatial organization of the P2Y11/AC/PKA/CaV1.2 nanodomain could be facilitated by scaffold proteins, such as A kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs).
evidence: This is a speculation based on known functions of AKAPs.

claim: AKAPs fine tune signal transduction by localizing GPCRs, signaling enzymes and effector proteins in close proximity to their substrates.
source: These AKAPs fine tune signal transduction by localizing GPCRs, signaling enzymes and effector proteins in close proximity to their substrates (Johnstone et al., 2018; Langeberg and Scott, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: AKAP150 (murine ortholog of human AKAP79) has been shown to interact with AC, PKA and CaV1.2.
source: The A kinase anchoring protein 150 (AKAP150; murine ortholog of human AKAP79) is of particular interest as it has been shown to interact with AC, PKA and CaV1.2 (Bauman et al., 2006; Efendiev et al., 2010; Gao et al., 1997; Murphy et al., 2014; Navedo et al., 2008; Nystoriak et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: AKAP79/150 can associate with multiple GPCRs.
source: Intriguingly, although AKAP79/150 can associate with multiple GPCRs (Fraser et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2011), no report to date has linked it to any purinergic receptor.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: AKAP79/150 is necessary for increased L-type Ca2+ channel activity in response to elevated glucose.
source: Localization of P2Y11 within the same AKAP79/150-driven complex may be critical as this scaffold protein is necessary for increased L-type Ca2+ channel activity in response to elevated glucose (Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior research.

claim: Glucose effects on LTCC activity and vascular reactivity require glucose transport into the cell and subsequent metabolism that can generate ATP.
source: Our recent study suggested that glucose effects on LTCC activity and vascular reactivity require glucose transport into the cell and subsequent metabolism that can generate ATP (Nystoriak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior research.

claim: ATP can be transported out of the cell through ATP-binding cassettes, vesicular exocytosis, plasma membrane F1F0-ATPase, connexin hemichannels and pannexin channels.
source: ATP can then be transported out of the cell through ATP-binding cassettes, vesicular exocytosis, plasma membrane F1F0-ATPase, connexin hemichannels and pannexin channels to induce activation of P2Y11 (Lohman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: One of the ATP transporters could form part of the AKAP/P2Y11/AC/PKA/CaV1.2 nanocomplex.
source: We thus speculate that one of these ATP transporters could form part of the AKAP/P2Y11/AC/PKA/CaV1.2 nanocomplex to provide another layer of compartmentalization that facilitates PKA-dependent regulation of LTCC function and vascular reactivity in response to elevations in extracellular glucose.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and known mechanisms of ATP release.

claim: Data start to define a unique nanomolecular complex likely formed by AKAP/P2Y11/AC/PKA/CaV1.2.
source: Data start to define a unique nanomolecular complex likely formed by AKAP/P2Y11/AC/PKA/CaV1.2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data.

claim: This nanocomplex can organize glucose signaling and help explain the intriguing consequences of glucose-induced PKA activation on LTCC function and vascular reactivity.
source: This nanocomplex can organize glucose signaling and help explain the intriguing consequences of glucose-induced PKA activation on LTCC function and vascular reactivity, which may have significant pathological implications, and therapeutic potential to treat vascular complications during diabetic hyperglycemia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data and its implications.

claim: P2Y11 can stimulate adenylyl cyclase (AC) activity to produce cAMP.
source: P2Y11 can stimulate adenylyl cyclase (AC) activity to produce cAMP (Communi et al., 1997; Kennedy, 2017; Schuchardt et al., 2012; von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: P2Y11 is known to associate with ACs to stimulate cAMP/PKA signaling.
source: Indeed, P2Y11 is known to associate with ACs to stimulate cAMP/PKA signaling (Communi et al., 1997; Pucéat et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: P2Y11 has been associated with positive inotropic effects of ATP on cardiomyocytes.
source: Current knowledge suggests that this receptor is associated with positive inotropic effects of ATP on cardiomyocytes and its activity seems to be impaired during cardiomyopathy (Balogh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: A polymorphism (Ala-87-Thr) in P2Y11 has been linked to increased risk of acute myocardial infarction and C-reactive protein blood levels.
source: Moreover, a polymorphism (Ala-87-Thr) in P2Y11 has been linked to increased risk of acute myocardial infarction and C-reactive protein blood levels (Amisten et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: ATP can activate P2Y11 with an EC50 that ranges from 1.8 to 17 μM, depending on the readout and the cell type used.
source: Indeed, ATP can activate P2Y11 with an EC50 that ranges from 1.8 to 17 μM, depending on the readout and the cell type used (Communi et al., 1999; Haas et al., 2014; Meis et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: P2Y11 can be activated by ATP/ATP-derived nucleotides with the following potency order: ATPγS > dATP > ATP>>>ADP.
source: Moreover, P2Y11 can be activated by ATP/ATP-derived nucleotides with the following potency order: ATPγS > dATP > ATP>>>ADP, with other nucleotides such as UTP and UDP having minimal or no influence on receptor activation (Kennedy, 2017; Schuchardt et al., 2012; von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: ATPγS stimulates P2Y11 activity with EC50 that ranges from 31 nM to 23 μM, depending on readout, cell type and species used.
source: Note that ATPγS stimulates P2Y11 activity with EC50 that ranges from 31 nM to 23 μM, depending on readout, cell type and species used, but it is still a more potent activator than ATP itself (Communi et al., 1999; Haas et al., 2014; Kennedy, 2017; Meis et al., 2010; Qi et al., 2001; Schuchardt et al., 2012; von Kügelgen and Harden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.
